name: Google Jules
description: Asynchronous cloud-VM coding agent from Google Labs, powered by Gemini (2.5/3 Pro for planning, Flash for lighter subtasks). Users assign well-defined tasks via the Jules web app, a CLI (Jules Tools), the Gemini CLI extension, or a GitHub issue label; Jules clones the repo into a dedicated isolated Google Cloud VM, plans, executes, tests, and delivers results as a GitHub pull request. Distinctive isolation policy: the VM retains network access (can npm install, run builds, call APIs), in contrast to OpenAI Codex's network-off sandbox.
user_identity_model: Google Sign-In (OAuth) is the primary account identity — no separate Jules account is created; users authenticate at jules.google.com with their Google account and grant access to basic profile info. GitHub OAuth is layered on top to authorize repository access (all repos or a selected subset). Identity is required (no device-local/anonymous mode). Higher task limits and stricter data-privacy terms (no training on private code) are tied to paid Google AI Pro and Ultra plans. The CLI (Jules Tools) and the Gemini CLI extension authenticate against the same Google-account-backed Jules service.
multi_user_collaboration: [uncertain] Jules is primarily a single-developer, account-scoped tool: tasks are tied to the signed-in Google account and its connected GitHub repos. Collaboration is mediated through GitHub itself — Jules opens PRs that any repo collaborator can review, approve, or request changes on, and an issue labeled 'jules' by any team member can trigger work. There is no documented in-product shared teamspace, role model, or org-isolation layer distinct from GitHub's own permissions; higher concurrency tiers come via Google AI Pro/Ultra subscriptions rather than a dedicated team-workspace construct.
workspace_definition: A workspace is effectively a connected GitHub repository (optionally scoped to specific branches/files via a file selector). It maps 1:1 to a git repo rather than a local filesystem path or a fully virtual abstract entity. Each task materializes the repo as a fresh checkout inside an isolated, short-lived Google Cloud VM. There is no persistent on-disk workspace owned by the user; the durable anchor is the GitHub repo plus a reusable environment snapshot associated with that repo.
workspace_session_binding: Sessions are scoped per task. Each task is bound to a (Google account, GitHub repo) pair and runs in its own dedicated VM, isolated from other tasks and conflicting dependencies. A user can run multiple concurrent tasks against the same or different repos simultaneously (3-60 concurrent depending on plan tier), so multiple active sessions per workspace are supported, each in its own VM. Tasks are tracked and resumable in the Jules dashboard / CLI until completion.
context_scoping: Repo-level context is derived from the cloned repository plus an AGENTS.md (and README.md) file at the repo root that Jules reads on every task to learn project structure, conventions, and tooling. Task-level context comes from the user's natural-language prompt, selected files, or a linked/labeled GitHub issue. There is no documented cross-repo global memory store; context is rebuilt per task from the repo, the AGENTS.md, and the prompt. An environment snapshot (filesystem/dependency state) is repo-scoped and reused across that repo's future tasks.
config_file_instruction_precedence: AGENTS.md at the repository root is the primary config/instruction file — Jules automatically looks for it and uses it to generate more relevant plans and completions. README.md is used as a secondary hint, especially for environment setup when no explicit setup script is provided. A user-supplied environment setup script (bash) governs how the VM is prepared for complex environments. [uncertain] No documented nested-directory override cascade or explicit file-size cap; precedence beyond AGENTS.md > README.md is not formally specified.
source_corpus_grounding_scope: Not applicable — Jules is a coding agent, not a research-assistant product. Its grounding corpus is the cloned source repository (code + AGENTS.md/README), not a curated document/source set like NotebookLM notebooks or Perplexity Spaces.
persistence_mechanism: [uncertain] Server-side managed by Google (no published storage schema). Durable persistence consists of: (1) the GitHub repository and the branch/PR Jules creates as the canonical output, and (2) a reusable environment snapshot of the VM's prepared filesystem/dependencies, stored and re-loaded for future tasks from that repo. The execution VM itself is ephemeral and short-lived — destroyed after task completion. Task metadata and plan/progress state are persisted in the Jules service for the dashboard and CLI, but the backing store (DB type, append-only vs mutable) is not publicly documented.
session_history: [uncertain] Task/session history is browsable in the Jules web dashboard and trackable via the CLI (progress, plan steps, completion/needs-input notifications). Each task records its plan, the visible step-by-step execution, and the resulting PR. The canonical, portable record of the work is the GitHub PR and branch (fully exportable via git). Internal storage format, retention policy, and whether the in-product activity log itself is exportable are not publicly documented.
memory_layering: Short-term memory is the per-task VM context (ephemeral, destroyed at teardown). Durable cross-task context is user-authored, not auto-generated: the repo-root AGENTS.md (and README.md) re-read on every task. Environment snapshots provide a durable filesystem/dependency layer reused across a repo's tasks. [uncertain] There is no documented auto-generated, evolving long-term memory store (in contrast to Windsurf/Claude auto-memory) — Jules rebuilds reasoning context per task from the repo plus AGENTS.md.
search_retrieval_history: [uncertain] Past tasks are listed/browsable in the dashboard, but there is no documented full-text or semantic search across historical sessions, nor an automatic mechanism to reference a prior session's conversation in a new task. Continuity across tasks is achieved indirectly via committed code in GitHub, the AGENTS.md file, and the repo's environment snapshot rather than via session-history retrieval.
lifecycle_ttl_cleanup: Strongly ephemeral execution model: each task runs in a short-lived VM that is destroyed after the task completes; uncommitted in-VM state not captured in the PR or snapshot is discarded at teardown. The environment snapshot is the deliberately persisted artifact that survives teardown and is reloaded to skip repeated setup. Plan-level task limits (per-day caps and concurrency caps, e.g., free tier 15 tasks/day & 3 concurrent up to top tier 60 concurrent) bound active sessions. [uncertain] No published explicit TTL/retention duration for completed task records.
sandbox_isolation_model: Each task runs in a dedicated, isolated, short-lived Google Cloud VM with a full Linux runtime (Node.js, Python, Go, Rust, Java, Ruby, PHP and common toolchains preinstalled). The repo is cloned into the VM; the agent has full filesystem access within the VM but cannot touch the developer's machine, and credentials/secrets stay under Google's control. Network access is ON by default — Jules can install dependencies, run builds/tests/linters, and call external APIs, explicitly contrasting with OpenAI Codex's network-off egress-blocked sandbox. Tasks are mutually isolated (separate VMs avoid dependency conflicts). Google states private code is not used to train Gemini models (under paid AI Pro/Ultra terms).
snapshot_state_restore: Yes — explicit environment snapshot feature. After running an environment setup script ('Run and Snapshot'), Jules captures a snapshot of the prepared VM environment (installed packages, configured filesystem state). That snapshot is stored against the repo and automatically reloaded for future tasks from that repo, skipping repetitive/long setup and improving consistency. This filesystem/env state is persisted independently of any conversation/task-history record, matching the Devin-snapshot / Codex-setup-script pattern.
cloud_local_handoff: Execution is cloud-only — all work happens in Google Cloud VMs; there is no local-execution or self-hosting mode. Surfaces (web app, Jules Tools CLI, Gemini CLI extension) are control planes that drive the same cloud-side tasks; the workload itself does not move to the user's local machine. The handoff to 'local' is via git: the user pulls the resulting branch/PR.
parallelism_subagent_fanout: Multiple independent tasks run in parallel, each in its own isolated VM, with concurrency capped by plan tier (e.g., free 3 concurrent, mid tiers 5-15, top tier up to 60 concurrent; daily task caps 15-100+). Parallel tasks isolate workspace state via separate VMs rather than sharing a workspace. [uncertain] No documented single-task internal subagent/coordinator fan-out (managed-Devins-style hierarchy); parallelism is at the task level, not an orchestrated multi-agent tree within one task.
trigger_surface: Multiple entry points: (1) Jules web app (jules.google.com) prompt box; (2) GitHub — labeling/mentioning an issue with the 'jules' tag triggers Jules to pick up the issue content as the task spec, and Jules can auto-detect and fix CI failures on its own PRs; (3) Jules Tools CLI (terminal companion); (4) the Gemini CLI extension that orchestrates Jules; (5) the jules-action GitHub Action for scheduled/CI workflows. This GitHub-event + CLI + web combination is the platform's distinctive trigger-surface mix.
implementation_stack: [uncertain] Largely undisclosed Google-managed backend. Known/observable components: Gemini models (2.5 Pro / 3 Pro for planning + reasoning, Gemini Flash for lighter subtasks; ~2M-token context window as of I/O 2026) as the reasoning engine; isolated Google Cloud VMs as the execution sandbox with network egress enabled; GitHub OAuth + the GitHub API (branches, commits, PRs, issue-label webhooks, GitHub Actions) as the integration/delivery layer; Google Sign-In (OAuth) for identity. Persistence layer (DB, session-store technology, event format) and snapshot-storage internals are not publicly documented.
applicability_to_labmate: Jules reinforces several Labmate design choices. (1) Identity: a federated OAuth identity (Google) decoupled from the work-source authorization (GitHub) maps to Labmate authenticating users (e.g., via Discord connector identity) separately from any per-tool/repo credential — keep user identity and resource-access tokens as distinct layers. (2) Workspace scoping: Jules anchors durable state to a stable external entity (the repo) while treating execution as ephemeral — analogous to Labmate using a stable workspace_id (the MongoDB session-doc anchor) while active session compute is transient (Redis Streams with TTL). (3) The AGENTS.md pattern is a clean precedent for a per-workspace, user-authored instruction file re-read on every run — a lighter alternative to auto-memory; Labmate could store an equivalent instruction blob on the workspace doc. (4) Snapshot reuse maps to caching prepared environment/state keyed by workspace_id to avoid re-setup, complementing Redis active-state checkpointing. (5) Trigger surface: the issue-mention -> async task -> PR loop is a strong model for Labmate's 'Discord message -> background LangGraph thread -> result delivered to channel' entry point; treat the inbound event (Discord mention) like Jules's issue label as the session-creation API surface, with thread_id checkpointing for resumability. (6) Note the network-ON isolation stance: if Labmate sessions need package installs / external API calls, an isolated-but-networked sandbox per session (vs network-off) is the precedent here.
